settings.title: What are mycotoxins?
settings.subtitle: Here is a comprehensive guide that includes definitions related to mycotoxins.

settings.question: What are mycotoxins?
settings.answer: Mycotoxins are invisible, toxic compounds produced by molds that contaminate crops like corn, wheat, oats, and nuts. They survive processing and cooking — and disrupt your gut, immune system, and neurological function over time

settings.question: Aflatoxins
settings.answer: Often found in corn, peanuts, and grains. Known carcinogen.

settings.question: Ochratoxin A
settings.answer: Detected in coffee, dried fruit, and cereals. Impacts kidneys and brain.

settings.question: Fumonisins
settings.answer: Especially in corn. Linked to neural defects and immune disruption.

settings.question: DON (Deoxynivalenol / Vomitoxin)
settings.answer: common in wheat and oats. Causes nausea and immune suppression.

settings.question: Zearalenone
settings.answer: Estrogen-mimicking toxin found in grains. Hormonal disruptor.

settings.question: Patulin
settings.answer: Often in Apple products. Linked to gut irritation and toxicity in children.

settings.question: T-2/HT-2 Toxins
settings.answer: Rare but potent, causing immune suppression and cellular damage.

settings.statement_text: The increasing threat of mycotoxin contamination in processed foods sheds light on why eating fresh, locally grown foods is essential to maintaining good health. These foods are also packed with vital nutrients and antioxidants that protect your body by helping it to filter out toxins. The following are some suggestions for improving your health and limiting dietary mycotoxin exposures.

settings.title: Processed foods
settings.description: Limit or eliminate your intake of processed and ultra-processed foods. Foods with many ingredients often go through multiple processing and packaging steps, increasing the risk of harmful mold and mycotoxin contamination. Be your own food processor by preparing meals from fresh farm ingredients and freezing leftovers. This reduces exposure to mold and toxins caused by additives, preservatives, plastics, and other processing methods.

settings.title: Water
settings.description: Use filtered water for cooking and drinking. Many health-compromising toxins, including mycotoxins, can find their way into drinking water.

settings.title: Cereal Grains
settings.description: Gluten grains often contain mycotoxins like DON, causing gastrointestinal issues. Fusarium infections have spread, leading to contamination in non-gluten grains like corn, oats, and rice. Consider removing grains such as wheat, corn, barley, oats, rye, sorghum, triticale, and rice, including cereals and pasta, for several weeks. Reintroduce less contaminated options like white rice, which loses some mycotoxins during processing but also loses prebiotic fiber. If missing grain-based foods, non-grain flours like tapioca, arrowroot, coconut, and almond flour are less contaminated and can be used to make bread and similar foods.

settings.title: Fruits and Vegetables
settings.description: Choose in-season, local fruits and vegetables for freshness. Select blemish-free produce, avoiding discoloration and soft spots. Opt for fresh, frozen, or freeze-dried options over dried varieties prone to mold. Berries like blueberries, blackberries, and raspberries boost phytochemicals and prebiotic fiber, helping prevent mycotoxin exposure. When possible, select organic produce for probiotic and prebiotic benefits. Incorporate cruciferous and leafy greens rich in mold toxin-eliminating compounds. Instead of commercial juices, make your own from fresh fruits and vegetables.

settings.title: Starchy and Root Vegetables
settings.description: Fresh, organic carrots, potatoes, sweet potatoes, and turnips provide energy and nutrients for a healthy lifestyle. They are rich in antioxidants and polyphenols that may protect against mycotoxin exposure but are also prone to mold-related diseases. Green-tinged skin, like on some potatoes, may indicate aflatoxin presence. Dark spots could mean Fusarium infection, containing trichothecene mycotoxins like DON. Always select fresh, healthy produce.

settings.title: Nuts and Nut Butter
settings.description: Buy whole fresh nuts, not pieces, as they are less prone to mycotoxin contamination. Avoid discolored nuts. Choose trusted brands that monitor mycotoxins, or make your own with fresh, cleaned nuts. Avoiding Aflatoxin from commercial nut butter can be difficult.

settings.title: Dairy Products
settings.description: Even pasture-fed animal milk can contain mycotoxins from silage, hay, and moldy cheese, which harbor toxins. Consider limiting dairy and cheese for a few weeks, and when reintroducing, make homemade yogurt with probiotic cultures to reduce mycotoxin effects like Aflatoxin M1 and Zearalenone. Non-dairy milks like oat milk are also at risk, requiring more testing and awareness for public safety.

settings.title: Meats
settings.description: Eat pasture-raised meat, fowl, and wild-caught fish whenever possible. Pasture-raised meats may contain fewer toxins. Avoid processed meats completely, as even the spices used during processing can be moldy.

settings.title: Herbs and Spices
settings.description: Use fresh spices and herbs instead of dried ones whenever possible. Dried herbs and spices can be contaminated with multiple mycotoxins. Cinnamon, oregano, garlic, turmeric, and a few other dried spices have antifungal properties and are probably okay to use instead of fresh. Once a container of dried herbs or spices is opened, store it in a dehumidified refrigerator or freezer to keep it fresh.

settings.title: Cooking Oils
settings.description: Avoid pro-inflammatory seed oils like canola, corn, and soybean because they can contain mycotoxins and other toxins. Instead, choose anti-inflammatory oils high in monounsaturated fats and polyphenols, such as extra virgin olive oil and avocado oil, for cooking and baking.

settings.title: Coffee, Tea, and Cocoa
settings.description: Tea and coffee are both moldy crops. Stick to brands that test for mycotoxins and take steps to prevent their occurrence, like Purity Coffee. Cocoa can be contaminated with ochratoxin A and aflatoxin. Addictive Wellness Chocolate tests their cacao for mycotoxins.

settings.title: Alcoholic Beverages
settings.description: There is no way to prevent mycotoxin exposure from alcoholic beverages, and the distillation process does not completely remove them. Grain-based drinks are susceptible to contamination with DON, zearalenone, and ochratoxin A, among others. Some wine companies test for mycotoxins and other contaminants, and more companies have entered the market recently (e.g., Dry Farm Wines).

settings.title: Sweeteners
settings.description: Replace refined commercial sugars that support fungal growth with honey or pure maple syrup. Honey and pure maple syrup serve as excellent sweeteners for cooking and baking. Both can help improve your microbiome and gut health and possess healing properties.

settings.text: Mycotoxins are external threats that can be mitigated by maintaining a healthy microbiome, which is populated by trillions of beneficial microbes. Including fermented foods such as sauerkraut, kimchi, or coconut/almond milk yogurt in your daily diet, and taking a high-quality probiotic, can help foster a healthier gut.
